articles.title: Those SMS Codes You Use to Log In to Your Accounts Are on Their Way Out—Here’s What You’ll Need to Do Instead
articles.content:
We all know the drill. You go to log into your bank, work email or favorite news website only to be met with a little pop-up blocking your access until you input an SMS code, a form of two-factor authentication. Would you like that code sent to your phone via text or email? Is your phone even near you, or charged? Well, you’d better hurry! It expires in 10 minutes.
Now, just when we finally got used to logging in this way, big changes are coming. (Sigh.) In fact, they’re here already for one major company, at least for many of its products and sites. And you know how it goes in the tech world: Once one company does something, it’s only a matter of time before they all jump on the train.
Ahead, I’ll walk you through the latest change to online security measures, tell you what’s replacing SMS verifications and explain how the new paradigm will affect you going forward. Keep reading to learn more and get ahead of the changing tech landscape.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more tech, travel, entertainment, humor and fun facts all week long.
Not yet. Microsoft is leading the charge here. The company recently announced that the familiar text codes will be phased out for personal Microsoft accounts, including Outlook, MSN and Hotmail, as well as other Windows applications and products like XBox, Windows PCs and Skype.
In addition to personal accounts, Microsoft announced the impending retirement of SMS codes for organizations that use Microsoft products. If you use Outlook or another MS product at work or school, you may have already begun seeing this change.
Other companies that are encouraging users to move away from SMS authentication include OpenAI, which announced earlier this year that users will be given the option to switch to another form of verification, and Google, which still supports SMS codes but is also pushing users to use other options.
It’s all about security. According to Microsoft, SMS verification is a huge source of fraud. The thing is, text messages are not that secure—telephone and cellular networks were just not designed to keep information sent in plain-text messages out of prying eyes.
And scammers have several ways to trick you into giving up your code. The biggest one is called SIM-card swapping. This is when fraudsters convince a mobile carrier to transfer your SIM card to them, log in to your accounts and intercept the SMS code that is sent for authentication. A Texas man was just convicted of this kind of fraud, sentenced to 70 months in prison and ordered to pay $1.7 million in restitution to victims. Last year, a Florida man was sentenced to 10 years in prison for similar crimes involving 59 separate victims. According to the FBI, this kind of SMS fraud cost consumers $26 million in 2024.
Aside from SIM-card swapping, relying on text messages to verify your account credentials sets you up for phishing attacks. Scammers set up a fake page that looks like your bank, email or other account, then send you a text message to entice you to log in to the fake page. They capture your info, log in themselves and have you enter the SMS code that is sent to you. Text-message fraud cost consumers $470 million in 2024, according to the Federal Trade Commission (FTC).
Microsoft is starting to use passkeys instead of SMS codes. Passkeys are forms of multi-factor authentication that include Face ID, fingerprints or a special digital key that uses your device to prove it’s really you. They work through something called “public-key cryptography,” a private key that’s stored on your device (like your fingerprint or Face ID), and a public key that comes from the website you’re trying to log in to.
When you log in to your accounts, the private key and the public key challenge each other to verify that you are authorized to log in. So instead of using a password or code that goes out over an insecure text, your device itself stores the info and proves that the public key and private key match. Passkeys are resistant to fraud because they cannot be faked by external actors.
It’s easy. When you log in to your Microsoft account, you will be prompted to create a passkey. (It’s currently optional on personal accounts, so you can also choose to skip the new process for now.)
Here’s what to do:
Now what? The next time you attempt to sign in to your Microsoft account, you will not receive that SMS-code prompt or that 10-minute countdown. Instead, you’ll be asked to provide the passkey you created directly on your phone or device, whether that’s your Face ID, fingerprint, PIN or security key.
Microsoft is already phasing out the old SMS codes, so you’ve likely seen the prompt window when you log in. For workplaces and other organizations, Microsoft plans to have everyone moved over to passkeys by July 2027. But the company has not made a public announcement about when the old codes will be 100% obsolete for personal accounts.
So for now, you can continue to ignore the prompt to create a passkey. But after learning how easy it is for scammers to infiltrate your accounts using SMS codes, you might want to create one sooner rather than later.

Text-message fraud cost consumers $470 million in 2024, according to the Federal Trade Commission (FTC).

It’s easy. When you log in to your Microsoft account, you will be prompted to create a passkey. (It’s currently optional on personal accounts, so you can also choose to skip the new process for now.)

Here’s what to do:

  1. Click on the “Sign in faster” button when prompted.
  2. Alternatively, go directly to Advanced Security Options if you’re already logged in.
  3. Choose “Add a new way to sign in or verify.”
  4. Select Face, Fingerprint, PIN or Security Key.
  5. Follow the instructions to create the passkey of your choosing.
  6. Select “Save” to store the passkey where suggested, or “Change” to store the passkey in another location.

Now what? The next time you attempt to sign in to your Microsoft account, you will not receive that SMS-code prompt or that 10-minute countdown. For workplaces and other organizations, Microsoft plans to have everyone moved over to passkeys by July 2027. But the company has not made a public announcement about when the old codes will be 100% obsolete for personal accounts.

So for now, you can continue to ignore the prompt to create a passkey. But after learning how easy it is for scammers to infiltrate your accounts using SMS codes, you might want to create one sooner rather than later.

articles.title: Social Security Just Announced a Cost-of-Living Increase for 2027—Here’s How Much Will Be in Those Checks
articles.content:
Social Security provides a lifeline for millions of people every month. And it’s not just retirees, though many older people rely on these monthly stipends. Younger people are also directly affected by Social Security news, whether they’re getting close to retirement, taking care of their parents or grandparents, or working with people who receive these benefits.
In fact, anyone who works and pays into Social Security, which is primarily financed through payroll taxes, has reason to pay attention to the latest news coming out of the Social Security Administration (SSA). Every year around this time, the SSA reveals the annual cost-of-living increase that will appear on the monthly checks—and you’ll definitely want to pay attention to this latest change.
The 2027 benefit-increase announcement couldn’t have come at a better time. Inflation is high, gas prices are way up and Americans of all ages are feeling the pinch. The increase will apply to both regular Social Security payments as well as Supplemental Security Income (SSI), which provides cash to people of any age who are blind, have disabilities or have limited sources of income.
So how much will this year’s increase be, and who will benefit? Will it make a dent in your retirement costs? And if you’re still many years away from that happy day, how can you make sure you’re planning for the future? Read on to find out and get some important advice from Social Security, retirement and money experts.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more money, work, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
The cost-of-living increase is just what it sounds like—adjustments to Social Security payments based on increased costs of basic expenses.
“The cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, was enacted by Congress as part of the 1972 Social Security Amendments, and automatic annual COLAs began in 1975,” explains Kevin Walton, a registered Social Security analyst certified by the National Association of Social Security Analysts. “Before that, benefits were increased only when Congress enacted special legislation.”
Since then, COLA has become something all beneficiaries count on each year. “The Social Security cost-of-living adjustment is an annual increase to every recipient’s benefits based on the change in the consumer price index over the past year,” says certified financial planner Stephen Kates, the principal financial analyst for the site RetireGuide.
The just-announced increase for 2027 will be 3.6%, which is the biggest jump since 2023. Individual amounts will depend on what your number is currently, but the SSA says the average increase will be about $75 per check.
Current retirees or recipients can take the gross monthly amount on their check and multiply it by 1.036 to determine 2027’s payments. This will give you your new gross check amount.
Here’s an example: Let’s say your 2026 monthly gross payments are $2,000. Multiplying $2,000 by 1.036 gives you a new total of $2,072. You can also determine the increase alone by multiplying $2,000 by 0.036 (aka 3.6%), which comes to $72.
For younger folks who haven’t yet started receiving Social Security, you can determine your eligible benefits by creating an account on SSA.gov, says Kates.
For the nearly 72 million regular Social Security recipients, the SSA will start sending checks with the new amounts in January 2027. For those on SSI, which is about 7.3 million people, the adjustment will start on Dec. 31, 2026.
It can be tough. According to Amie Clark of The Senior List, a website focused on aging-related consumer news, nearly 30% of retirees are not confident they’ll be able to maintain their current lifestyle throughout retirement. “The most unexpected financial challenges for retirees [are] inflation and rising living costs, followed closely by medical and health-care expenses and home-repair and maintenance costs,” she says.
Here are some expert-approved strategies to help stretch your retirement dollars or save money at any age.
Managing cash flow is important for everyone, but for retired folks, limiting spending to only what is coming in from Social Security, investments and part-time jobs is critical. “Maintain a budget for your spending, and plan ahead for future spending,” Kates advises.
Then focus on saving. After all, it’s much less stressful to save for a rainy day than spend sleepless nights worrying about debt from impulse purchases. When you have a little extra, save it if you can. “In years when investments are performing well, emergency funds can be boosted,” he says. “These will be important for years when your investments perform poorly and will offer you assets to draw from with little risk or tax consequences.”
There’s a rush that comes with shopping and getting new things, but in some cases, you can refresh what you have, which is also good for the environment. “In day-to-day spending, capitalize on opportunities to save on the everyday things you plan to do anyway,” Kates suggests. “Credit card rewards, rebates, home-maintenance tax rebates and more are all available to retirees who seek them out.”
It’s a good idea to look at your fixed expenses, make sure they’re really “fixed” and see if you can cut costs without too much sacrifice. “This can include reevaluating your auto and home insurance or eliminating the number of times you eat out each week,” says Chuck Czajka, a certified Social Security claiming strategist and the founder of Macro Money Concepts in Stuart, Florida.
Although debit cards come with their own risks, you want to be mindful of how much you’re charging. “When it comes to credit cards, keep usage to a minimum,” Czajka advises. “If you do make credit card charges, ensure you pay them off in full at the end of each month.”
You may think you can manage your finances on your own, but it can be helpful to have an investment advisor or accountant help you with the big picture. You might even find that saving money can be a fun challenge! “There may be opportunities to plan withdrawals or asset sales in certain years to minimize future taxes or take advantage of certain allowable tax credits or deductions,” Kates says. A financial advisor or accountant can help you with that.
Nobody really wants to significantly delay retirement, but holding off on getting your Social Security benefits is a wise move. “For those who have not yet retired or claimed Social Security benefits, waiting until full retirement age or later can significantly increase retirement income,” Kates says. “If benefits are delayed, payments will increase by roughly 8% per year until age 70.”
Whether you’re dealing with long service agreements or cellphone contracts and bills, it’s critical to read the fine print. If you feel like you’re reading gobbledygook, you’re not alone. But ask a trusted relative or friend to help you. When all else fails, hire a lawyer.
About the experts
At Reader’s Digest, we’re committed to producing high-quality content by writers with expertise and experience in their field in consultation with relevant, qualified experts. We rely on reputable primary sources, including government and professional organizations and academic institutions as well as our writers’ personal experiences where appropriate. We verify all facts and data, back them with credible sourcing and revisit them over time to ensure they remain accurate and up to date. For this piece, Jaime Stathis tapped her experience as a longtime journalist who covers money, work and scams for Reader’s Digest to make sure all information is accurate and offers the best possible advice to readers. Read more about our team, our contributors and our editorial policies.

articles.title: Astrological Warning! We’re About to Get Hit with a Rare Double Retrograde—And These 4 Signs Will Have a Particularly Tough Time
articles.content:
Sometimes, astrology predictions hit in a way that could make anyone a believer. And this month has the power to do just that. In fact, just today, a client told me she didn’t believe in astrology until she read the October predictions I gave her. So even if you’re not totally sold on cosmic guidance (or you’re just a Capricorn), you’ll want to pay attention this month. October 2026 is filled with one of the rarest, most cataclysmic events that could dismantle the relationships you thought were strong and prompt the ghosts of exes past to pay you a visit.
That’s because October is hurtling two major retrogrades at us … at the same time … in the same sign. Quick astrology refresher: A retrograde planet signifies a time when that planet appears to be moving backward across the sky and isn’t operating to its fullest capacity. Things break, wires get crossed, items are lost, messages aren’t received. Astrologers like to focus on the “re” part of the word retrograde—return, revisit, reorganize, reconvene—because retrogrades have an eerie way of turning back time.
It’s already atypical to have two major planets doing this at the same time. But these two retrograde planets will have a particular interest in our love lives, and four signs will be hit the hardest. Read on to find out what you’re in store for—and whether you’re among the particularly unlucky ones.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more astrology, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
This rare double retrograde includes a Venus retrograde in Scorpio and Libra at the start of October, and then a Mercury retrograde in Scorpio later in the month. This will continue until Nov. 13, when both planets turn direct.
Aside from the two retrogrades happening at once, the specific signs the planets are traveling in play a big role. Scorpio rules secrets, obsession, alchemy and the hidden. This sign’s job is to surface the taboo, untouched things so we can learn from them. Now, apply that to the upcoming retrograde planets, and you get people pinging you to discuss old matters (Mercury, the planet of communication), especially about romantic relationships (Venus, the planet of love).
For most of the month, Venus retrograde will travel through Scorpio. On Oct. 24, Mercury turns retrograde in Scorpio. The planets share a retrograde period in Scorpio for one day. And then on Oct. 25, Venus will move into Libra, the literal sign of relationships. Here’s a quick breakdown:
A typical retrograde will never affect everyone the same way—or sometimes even at all. However, because there are two retrogrades happening concurrently, in two different signs, they’ll occupy more real estate in communal charts. And they will likely affect everyone’s relationships, though, as noted, some signs will feel it more than others. (More on that in a minute.)
For most of October, the Venus retrograde in Scorpio will push us into investigative mode. Since Venus rules both relationships and money, its placement in Scorpio encourages us to dig deep into our relationships and right certain wrongs related to money. But when it’s retrograde, it means we’re digging even deeper, specifically into our past relationships and connections or into past money issues.
The investigative mode is turned down slightly when Venus moves into Libra. However, this will act less as a reconnaissance period and more as a reconciliation period. This is when we use the information we’ve discovered to find healing, self-love and personal growth—away from relationships that we’ve held onto or that still hold us back.
Mercury retrograde’s entry at the end of the month brings more conversation around. So things are finally said, apologies are made, notice is given and endings begin.
Overall, the two retrogrades will push us to revisit conversations and experiences we’ve already had—especially with old partners.
While everyone will feel at least subtle effects this month, some zodiac signs will really feel the double whammy. The reason? If Venus or Mercury retrograde hits your personal sign, this means it’s traveling through a personal sector of your chart—and you’re bound to feel personally victimized by this retrograde season.
Both Venus and Mercury will be moving through your sign, Scorpio, which can feel really heavy. Thanks to this pressure, you’re going to feel very self-aware and perhaps self-scrutinizing as well. You’ll look back on your relationships and consider how you responded in each one. Were you fair? Was it equal? Do you actually need that apology, or should you be the one giving it?
Unpopular opinion: The best form of loving yourself is holding the version of you that was hurt, then moving on.
Both of these retrogrades are happening in the sector of your chart that rules serious, long-term relationships. So while some of the signs may have flings or “almost” partners sliding in their DMs, you’re most likely to hear from your BIG ex.
Now, this may sound jarring. But the point of their reentrance into your life is this: In order to choose yourself again, you need the option to choose them. So even if you’re not totally sold on cosmic guidance (or you’re just a Capricorn), you’ll want to pay attention this month. October 2026 is filled with one of the rarest, most cataclysmic events that could dismantle the relationships you thought were strong and prompt the ghosts of exes past to pay you a visit.

That’s because October is hurtling two major retrogrades at us … at the same time … in the same sign. Things break, wires get crossed, items are lost, messages aren’t received. Astrologers like to focus on the “re” part of the word retrograde—return, revisit, reorganize, reconvene—because retrogrades have an eerie way of turning back time.

It’s already atypical to have two major planets doing this at the same time. Scorpio

Unpopular opinion: The best form of loving yourself is holding the version of you that was hurt, then moving on.

Taurus

Both of these retrogrades are happening in the sector of your chart that rules serious, long-term relationships. So while some of the signs may have flings or “almost” partners sliding in their DMs, you’re most likely to hear from your BIG ex.

Their little “Hey, I’ve been thinking about you” message might have you daydreaming about what could be, but at the end of the day, has anything really changed? Probably not. Choose yourself. 

Libra

Venus retrograde won’t move into your sign until Oct. 25. So for most of October, the focus is on the part of your chart that rules the subconscious. Cancer

Especially because Mercury is turning backward here, you’re going to hear from old connections. Think: that person you met on Tinder and never heard from again, the summer fling you had back in college or that very brief almost-affair you got into with someone’s partner. What should you do to counter these effects?

Unfortunately, you can’t really do anything to improve this retrograde season. The cosmos will bring back what’s supposed to come back in the way you least expect. However, there are things you can do to prepare yourself for openness, personal strength and that possible conversation with an ex. 

To prepare for ex sightings and visitations, it’s helpful to remind yourself of the bad times, so that when they do reach out, you don’t immediately reach for the good memories. (Retrogrades can bring delusions, so it’s important to stay on top of this.) To do this, take screenshots of your three worst moments or memories with them, to pull up when you need them.

Ultimately, try not to make any rash decisions this October—and this will be challenging. The offer might look really good. Or your ex might say everything you’ve always wanted to hear. But whatever happens right now doesn’t usually stick for the long haul.

We often forget that this period is the test. This is why retrogrades aren’t for acting; they’re for pausing. So when an offer is made or someone reaches out, pause first. Sleep on it. This will remind you of what you actually want, so you’re not reacting with emotions first.

articles.title: Elon Musk Is Spending More Than $275 Million on the Midterm Elections. Did We Always Have This Much Money in Politics—And Is This Even Legal?
articles.content:
Since July, trillionaire Elon Musk has spent $276 million dollars on the upcoming midterm elections, according to the New York Times. He directed that astonishing amount of money to both his super political action committee (PAC) and Republican groups in a bid to stave off what is expected to be major losses for the party this fall.
Much of this money, about $158 million, went to the Senate Leadership Fund in an effort to maintain a majority in that chamber of Congress. Another big outlay, $76 million, went to Musk’s super PAC, which will spend the cash on canvassing for candidates in seven Senate races and dozens of House ones.
And that’s just since July. All in all, he has spent roughly $366 million dollars on the 2025–2026 election cycle. This isn’t the first time Musk has made influential campaign contributions either. He spent more than $290 million on the 2024 election, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings—more than any other donor.
As of the latest FEC filings from July, PACs from all parties had raised $8.3 billion and spent $6.5 billion during the 2025–2026 election cycle. (The FEC filing deadline is coming up on Oct. 15, 2026, so these numbers are even higher now.) It’s hard to believe that it’s legal for people like Musk to spend these staggering amounts to influence elections, but thanks to a landmark 2010 Supreme Court ruling, it is.
Ahead, we spoke with politics and election-law experts Jen Heerwig, PhD, Donald Tobin, JD, and Alex Keena, PhD, to understand this consequential (and controversial) court case. Read on to learn more about the influence of money in politics and how this case changed campaign spending.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more election news, tech, humor, travel and fun facts all week long.
In inflation-adjusted terms, the elections of 2020 broke all records: Nearly $19 billion was spent on the presidential race and congressional races combined, says Heerwig, an associate professor of sociology at SUNY-Stony Brook who studies political contributions by American corporate elites. In 2016, that number was less than $10 billion. “It’s unusual to see the cost of elections nearly double in the space of four years,” she says.
One reason for this increase is the gradual influx of super PACs, Heerwig explains. “In 2016, over $1 billion was spent by super PACs. In 2020, over $2 billion was spent by these groups.” A large proportion of this money goes to political advertising, which is getting more expensive every year.
That said, the composition of spending in our elections had been changing even before the explosion of money in 2020. And as you’ll see coming up, there’s a reason why super PACs have become such an important driver of election spending.
The driving force behind this substantial shift in campaign contributions was a 2010 Supreme Court case, Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission, which allowed corporations to spend unlimited sums of money to support or oppose a candidate running for federal office.
“Previously, corporations had to establish a PAC, which could only spend $5,000 giving to a particular candidate under the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971,” according to Keena, an associate professor of political science at Virginia Commonwealth University who focuses on money in politics and elections. “The Supreme Court said that part of the law was unconstitutional because it violated the ‘political speech’ rights of corporations.”
Essentially, the Supreme Court reasoned that corporations should have the First Amendment right to speak in elections. “After Citizens United, a private company could decide to make an advertisement to support the candidacy of, say, Donald Trump or a candidate running for the U.S. House or Senate,” Heerwig says. “Since there are no limits on independent expenditures, a company could spend unlimited amounts to support its favored candidates, so long as it did so on its own.”
The ruling has had a predictable influence on our elections. “Since the Citizens United ruling, super PACs have gradually become more important in election spending,” Heerwig says.
The Citizens United ruling created a new type of PAC—a super PAC—that can give unlimited money but cannot directly “coordinate” with a campaign. “In practice, this requirement is unenforced,” Keena explains. “For example, Elon Musk created a super PAC to help Trump win in 2024, and he was in frequent contact with the Trump campaign and even appeared on stage with Trump when he was a candidate.”
Interestingly, Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission began in the lower courts as a case about what kinds of information must be disclosed by entities making political advertisements and communications, Heerwig explains. But the U.S. Supreme Court’s consideration of the case revolved around the ban on corporate independent spending—contributions made directly from company treasuries to influence elections, like a political advertisement made to support or oppose a candidate for the U.S. House or Senate, she notes.
This massive shift in contributions makes candidates, campaigns and political parties more reliant on corporate and monied interests, Keena says. “The increase in money being spent means candidates have to spend more of their time asking the rich for donations, and in response, the political parties have become more responsive to the interests of the wealthy and special interests that support them,” he explains.
The result? Congress now gives preferential treatment to the ideas and policies favored by the donor class and makes symbolic overtures to ordinary citizens rather than offering substantive representation, Keena says.
Super PAC spending tends to target the most competitive races, where spending even a small amount of money may be more meaningful, Heerwig says. “In these races, we’ve seen super PACs inundate media markets with advertisements of all types—online, print, television, etc.,” she explains.
Yes, it’s totally legal for Elon Musk to channel hundreds of millions of dollars into our elections through his super PAC. “The courts view this money as a constitutional right,” Keena says. “All Americans are entitled to spend as much as they want on election advertising and communications.”
However, Musk’s super PAC can’t coordinate with official candidate committees, Heerwig says. But that restriction doesn’t have much bite these days. “In practice, we know that super PACs can and do coordinate with candidates, and our chief federal election watchdog, the Federal Election Commission, has not meaningfully intervened,” she explains.
It’s important to recognize that Elon Musk could spend unlimited dollars on the midterms prior to Citizens United as long as he did not coordinate with any candidate, says Tobin, an election and tax law professor and former dean of the University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law. What Citizens United did was allow Musk to make such contributions through a corporate form.
“In reality, it had no serious impact on an individual’s ability to spend unlimited funds,” he explains. “It just made it easier because Musk can create an independent expenditure PAC and he can just contribute to that PAC.”
Yes, it’s possible that the Citizens United ruling will be reversed at some point, Keena says.
If (or when) the membership of the Supreme Court changes (such as through death, resignation or future expansion) or when societal attitudes change, “future courts could reverse this ruling,” Keena says. “Otherwise, reversing it would require a constitutional amendment.”
Alternatively, Congress could pass legislation creating a different regulatory system for campaign contributions, Tobin says.
As the 2026 midterm elections approach, keep an eye out for the signs that big money is at play. Keena recommends looking at who is giving money to the candidates as well as the super PAC money being spent to support them. “This money creates relationships of obligations between politicians and their financiers, and it previews what types of policies a politician might support or oppose in office,” he explains.
If you live in a state or district with a competitive race, Heerwig suggests paying very careful attention to the disclaimer that appears at the end of political advertisements. “If the advertisement does not explicitly contain the endorsement of the named candidate, then it’s an ad that’s been funded by a third-party group, likely a super PAC,” she explains. “Stay vigilant about fact-checking the claims coming from these groups.”

articles.title: This Food Is Actually Healthier as a Leftover—Can You Guess What It Is?
articles.content:
In my house, we try to have a home-cooked dinner at least five nights a week. That said, we’ve learned that the only way this is remotely achievable is to choose at least one meal that makes enough to eat twice—once fresh out of the oven or off the stovetop, and again as leftovers later in the week. A lot of the time, this is soup. (We’re a big soup household.) But the second-most-common dish we have on leftovers night is one that’s actually healthier for you to eat one or two days after cooking.
Yes, you heard that right. There’s one beloved food that’s better for you if you cook it and then pop it in the fridge for a day or two before eating it. What kind of sorcery is this? The wonderful kind!
Keep reading to find out what this magical food is—and what kind of special alchemy happens in your fridge when it spends the night in there.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more food news, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
Ever heard of lasagna? Spaghetti and meatballs? Penne a la vodka? I could go on—I do love my pasta. And that’s a good thing because pasta is the food I’m talking about. It’s actually much healthier when it’s eaten as leftovers, and it’s all because of what happens to the starch molecules that make up the pasta during both the cooking and cooling processes.
“When pasta cooks, its starch granules absorb water, and [they] swell,” explains Jordan Langhough, a registered dietitian and certified personal trainer in Charlotte, North Carolina. “This process makes it easier for your body to break down the starch quickly and turn it into glucose.”
But then, as your hot pasta cools, something else happens. “When it cools, those starch molecules go through a process called retrogradation: They reorganize into a tighter, more crystalline structure that your digestive enzymes can’t break down as easily,” Langhough says. This new structure that’s formed is called resistant starch—and it is the key to all the potential health benefits you can get from leftover pasta.
“Resistant starch acts more like fiber than a carb in the body,” says Langhough. What does that mean? When you eat simple carbs, like white bread or cookies, your body immediately breaks them down, sending glucose (aka sugar) straight into your bloodstream, and that can cause a host of problems. Fiber, on the other hand, travels through your digestive system without being broken down, which leads to a variety of possible perks, including the following.
During digestion, resistant starch isn’t broken down in the stomach like simpler carbs are. Instead, explains Langhough, it travels to the large intestine, where it acts as a prebiotic, or a food that nourishes the beneficial bacteria that live there. This allows the healthy bacteria in your gut to thrive. Studies have shown that people with a healthier, more diverse microbiome have lower cholesterol levels, higher fitness levels and greater longevity than those who don’t have as many good bugs living in their gut. That’s because these bacteria influence everything from digestion to disease prevention.
On the flip side, if your microbiome is overrun by bad bugs, you can experience digestive difficulties, an increased risk of inflammatory bowel diseases, fatigue, mood changes and more, according to the Cleveland Clinic. The bottom line: You want your gut microbiome to be as healthy as possible, and eating foods rich in resistant starch is an excellent way to support that goal.
Resistant starch reduces the glycemic impact of the meal, or how quickly the food causes your blood sugar to rise, says Langhough. While hot pasta contains simple starches that are broken down quickly, causing a rapid rise, the resistant starch in leftover pasta is not broken down at all, slowing the spike that your meal creates.
This is a big deal for people with diabetes who are trying to avoid blood-sugar spikes. According to one study in the Journal of Diabetes Investigation, resistant starch seems to lower post-meal blood-sugar levels, making it a promising part of medical nutrition therapy for type 2 diabetes.
That said, avoiding blood-sugar spikes is smart for everyone. Frequent extreme spikes and dips in those levels can contribute to increased inflammation, low energy, poor sleep, irritability and possibly even an increased risk of cancer, according to a 2025 review. You also tend to feel hungry again after a spike and drop in blood sugar, which can lead to snacking and subsequent weight gain. It’s best to keep your blood sugar as steady as possible.
“Over time, regularly eating resistant starch has been linked to a greater sense of fullness after eating,” Langhough says. That’s primarily because it travels through the GI tract without breaking down, so you’ll feel fuller for longer, potentially delaying your next meal or snack and reducing your overall food intake for the day.

Ever heard of lasagna? Spaghetti and meatballs? Penne a la vodka? I could go on—I do love my pasta. And that’s a good thing because pasta is the food I’m talking about. It’s actually much healthier when it’s eaten as leftovers, and it’s all because of what happens to the starch molecules that make up the pasta during both the cooking and cooling processes.

“When pasta cooks, its starch granules absorb water, and [they] swell,” explains Jordan Langhough, a registered dietitian and certified personal trainer in Charlotte, North Carolina. “This process makes it easier for your body to break down the starch quickly and turn it into glucose.”

“Resistant starch acts more like fiber than a carb in the body,” says Langhough. What does that mean? When you eat simple carbs, like white bread or cookies, your body immediately breaks them down, sending glucose (aka sugar) straight into your bloodstream, and that can cause a host of problems. Fiber, on the other hand, travels through your digestive system without being broken down, which leads to a variety of possible perks, including the following.

Instead, explains Langhough, it travels to the large intestine, where it acts as a prebiotic, or a food that nourishes the beneficial bacteria that live there. This allows the healthy bacteria in your gut to thrive. Studies have shown that people with a healthier, more diverse microbiome have lower cholesterol levels, higher fitness levels and greater longevity than those who don’t have as many good bugs living in their gut. That’s because these bacteria influence everything from digestion to disease prevention.

On the flip side, if your microbiome is overrun by bad bugs, you can experience digestive difficulties, an increased risk of inflammatory bowel diseases, fatigue, mood changes and more, according to the Cleveland Clinic. The bottom line: You want your gut microbiome to be as healthy as possible, and eating foods rich in resistant starch is an excellent way to support that goal.

That said, avoiding blood-sugar spikes is smart for everyone. Frequent extreme spikes and dips in those levels can contribute to increased inflammation, low energy, poor sleep, irritability and possibly even an increased risk of cancer, according to a 2025 review. You also tend to feel hungry again after a spike and drop in blood sugar, which can lead to snacking and subsequent weight gain. It’s best to keep your blood sugar as steady as possible.

  • Rice and potatoes: “The same principle applies,” says Langhough. “Cook them, cool them in the fridge, and they develop significantly more resistant starch than when eaten hot.”
  • Beans and lentils: “These are naturally high in resistant starch, and they get an additional boost when cooled,” Langhough says.
